In this article, we develop a general technique for gluing subcategories of $\infty$-categories. We obtain categorical equivalences between simplicial sets associated to certain multisimplicial sets. Such equivalences can be used to construct functors in different contexts. One of our results generalizes Deligne's gluing theory developed in the construction of the extraordinary pushforward operation in étale cohomology of schemes. Our results are applied in subsequent articles to construct Grothendieck's six operations in étale cohomology of Artin stacks.

Introduction The extraordinary pushforward, one of Grothendieck’s six operations, in étale cohomology of schemes was constructed in SGA 4 XVII [ 6 ] . Let 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} be the category of quasi-compact and quasi-separated schemes, with morphisms being separated of finite type, and let Λ \Lambda be a fixed torsion ring. For a morphism f : Y → X f\colon Y\to X in 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} , the extraordinary pushforward by f f is a functor f ! : D ( Y , Λ ) → D ( X , Λ ) , \displaystyle f_{!}\colon\mathrm{D}(Y,\Lambda)\to\mathrm{D}(X,\Lambda), between unbounded derived categories of Λ \Lambda -modules in the étale topoi. The functoriality of this operation is encoded by a pseudofunctor F : 𝒮 ​ ch ′ → 𝒞 ​ at 1 \displaystyle F\colon\mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime}\to\mathcal{C}\mathrm{at}_{1} sending a scheme X X in 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} to D ⁡ ( X , Λ ) \mathrm{D}(X,\Lambda) and a morphism f : Y → X f\colon Y\to X in 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} to the functor f ! f_{!} . Here 𝒞 ​ at 1 \mathcal{C}\mathrm{at}_{1} denotes the ( 2 , 1 ) (2,1) -category of categories 1 1 1 A ( 2 , 1 ) (2,1) -category is a 2 2 -category in which all 2 2 -cells are invertible. . There are obvious candidates for the restrictions F P F_{P} and F J F_{J} of F F to the subcategories 𝒮 ​ ch P ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime}_{P} and 𝒮 ​ ch J ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime}_{J} of 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} spanned respectively by proper morphisms and open immersions. The construction of F F thus amounts to gluing the two pseudofunctors. For this, Deligne developed a general theory for gluing two pseudofunctors of target 𝒞 ​ at 1 \mathcal{C}\mathrm{at}_{1} [ 6 ] *Section 3. Deligne’s gluing theory, together with its variants ( [ 1 ] *Section 1.3, [ 23 ] ), have found several other applications ( [ 1 ] , [ 3 ] , [ 24 ] ). In the present article, we study the problem of gluing in higher categories. The technique developed here can be used to construct Grothendieck’s six operations in different contexts ( [ 19 , 18 ] , [ 22 ] ). In [ 19 , 18 ] , we use the gluing technique to construct higher categorical six operations in étale cohomology of higher Artin stacks and prove the base change theorem. Even for 1 1 -Artin stacks and ordinary six operations, this theorem was previously only established on the level of sheaves (and subject to other restrictions) [ 16 , 17 ] . Our construction of the six operations makes essential use of higher categorical descent, so that even if one is only interested in the six operations and base change in ordinary derived categories, the enhanced version is still an indispensable step of the construction. As a starting point for the descent procedure, we need an enhancement of the pseudofunctor F F above. In the language of ∞ \infty -categories [ 20 ] , such an enhancement is a functor F ∞ : N ⁡ ( 𝒮 ​ ch ′ ) → 𝒞 ​ at ∞ \displaystyle F^{\infty}\colon\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime})\to\mathcal{C}\mathrm{at}_{\infty} between ∞ \infty -categories, where N ⁡ ( 𝒮 ​ ch ′ ) \mathrm{N}(\mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime}) is the nerve of 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} and 𝒞 ​ at ∞ \mathcal{C}\mathrm{at}_{\infty} denotes the ∞ \infty -category of ∞ \infty -categories. For every scheme X X in 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} , F ∞ ​ ( X ) F^{\infty}(X) is an ∞ \infty -category 𝒟 ⁡ ( X , Λ ) \mathcal{D}(X,\Lambda) , whose homotopy category is equivalent to D ⁡ ( X , Λ ) \mathrm{D}(X,\Lambda) . For every morphism f : Y → X f\colon Y\to X in 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} , the image F ∞ ​ ( f ) F^{\infty}(f) is a functor f ! ∞ : 𝒟 ( Y , Λ ) → 𝒟 ( X , Λ ) f_{!}^{\infty}\colon\mathcal{D}(Y,\Lambda)\to\mathcal{D}(X,\Lambda) such that the induced functor h f ! ∞ \mathrm{h}f_{!}^{\infty} between homotopy categories is equivalent to the classical f ! f_{!} . One major difficulty of the construction of F ∞ F^{\infty} is the need to keep track of coherence of all levels. By Nagata compactification [ 4 ] , every morphism f f in 𝒮 ​ ch ′ \mathcal{S}\mathrm{ch}^{\prime} can be factorized as p ∘ j p\circ j , where j j is an open immersion and p p is proper. One can then define F ⁡ ( f ) F(f) as F P ​ ( p ) ∘ F J ​ ( j ) F_{P}(p)\circ F_{J}(j) . The issue is that such a factorization is not canonical, so that one needs to include coherence with composition as part of the data. Since the target of F F is a ( 2 , 1 ) (2,1) -category, in Deligne’s theory coherence up to the level of 2 2 -cells suffices. The target of F ∞ F^{\infty} being an ∞ \infty -category, we need to consider coherence of all levels. Another complication is the need to deal with more than two subcategories. This need is already apparent in [ 24 ] . We will give another illustration in the proof of Corollary 0.4 below. To handle these complications, we propose the following general framework. Let us illustrate them in the case of Corollary 0.2 . The map g g can be decomposed as δ 2 ∗ ​ N ​ ( 𝒞 ) ℰ 1 , ℰ 2 cart → g ′ δ 2 ∗ ​ N ​ ( 𝒞 ) ℰ 1 , ℰ 2 → g ′′ N ⁡ ( 𝒞 ) , \delta_{2}^{*}\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C})_{\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2}}^{\mathrm{cart}}\xrightarrow{g^{\prime}}\delta_{2}^{*}\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C})_{\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2}}\xrightarrow{g^{\prime\prime}}\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C}), where δ 2 ∗ ​ N ​ ( 𝒞 ) ℰ 1 , ℰ 2 \delta_{2}^{*}\mathrm{N}(\mathcal{C})_{\mathcal{E}_{1},\mathcal{E}_{2}} is the simplicial set whose n n -simplices are diagrams ( Introduction ) without the requirement that every square is Cartesian, g ′ g^{\prime} is the natural inclusion and g ′′ g^{\prime\prime} is the map remembering the diagonal. We prove that both g ′ g^{\prime} and g ′′ g^{\prime\prime} are categorical equivalences. The fact that g ′′ g^{\prime\prime} is a categorical equivalence is an ∞ \infty -categorical generalization of Deligne’s result [ 6 ] *Proposition 3.3.2. The article is organized as follows. In Section 1 , we collect some basic definitions and facts in the theory of ∞ \infty -categories [ 20 ] for the reader’s convenience. In Section 2 , we develop a general technique for constructing functors to ∞ \infty -categories. The method will be used several times in this article and its sequels [ 19 , 18 ] . In Section 3 , we introduce several notions related to multisimplicial sets used in the statements of our main results. In particular, we define the restricted multisimplicial nerve of an ∞ \infty -category with extra data. In Section 4 , we prove a multisimplicial descent theorem, which implies that the map g ′′ g^{\prime\prime} is a categorical equivalence. In Section 5 , we prove a Cartesian gluing theorem, which implies that the inclusion g ′ g^{\prime} is a categorical equivalence. A Cartesian gluing formalism for pseudofunctors between 2 2 -categories was developed in [ 23 ] . Our treatment here is quite different and more adapted to the higher categorical context. In Section 6 , we prove some facts about inclusions of simplicial sets used in the previous sections. Conventions Unless otherwise specified, a category is to be understood as an ordinary category. We will not distinguish between sets and categories in which the only morphisms are identity morphisms. For categories 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , we let Fun ⁡ ( 𝒞 , 𝒟 ) \mathrm{Fun}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D}) denote the category of functors from 𝒞 \mathcal{C} to 𝒟 \mathcal{D} , whose objects are functors and whose morphisms are natural transformations. We let id \mathrm{id} denote various identity morphisms. Throughout this article, an effort has been made to keep our notation consistent with those in [ 20 ] .
